Excellencies, distinguished delegates, good afternoon. On behalf of my co-chair, Ms. Shoko Noda, Assistant Secretary-General, Assistant Administrator and Director of the Crisis Bureau of the United Nations Development Programme, and on my own behalf, It is my honor and privilege to welcome you all to Session 4 of the 2026 High-Level Conference, Heads of Counterterrorism Agencies of Member States. A warm welcome to our special guests and distinguished panelists, to representatives of member states, to our colleagues from across the United Nations system, and to representatives of regional and international organizations joining us today. This session, dedicated to Strategic Capacity Building Responses: Countering Misuse of Artificial Intelligence and New Emerging Technologies, This session focuses on one of the most rapidly evolving dimensions of the, of the contemporary counterterrorism landscape. Technological innovation presents significant opportunities for prevention, preparedness, and response. At the same time, terrorist groups continue to exploit digital platforms, artificial intelligence, unmanned systems, encrypted communications, and other emerging technologies to enhance their capabilities, expand their reach, and adapt their operational models. Addressing these challenges, requires sustained international cooperation, effective capacity-building support, and responsible approaches to innovation that uphold international law, human rights, and the rule of law. We look forward to a rich and substantive discussion. Before we proceed to our speakers, my co-chair and I will each deliver brief remarks in our respective capacities. Allow me to switch in Arabic for my remarks.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the world is witnessing accelerating developments in the field of new and emerging technologies. Terrorist groups are growing more capable of exploiting these tools to recruit, spread extremist propaganda, raise funding, and plot terrorist operations. We must strengthen countries' preparedness and national capabilities to keep pace with these evolving threats. The Kingdom believes that capacity building is a key pillar to combat terrorism and extremism. Success in counterterrorism effort hinges not only on security measures but also requires strong national institutions, efficient legal frameworks, close international cooperation, and sustained investment in human and technical capacity development. The Kingdom was keen to support capacity-building effort nationally, regionally, and internationally. In 2011, we contributed to the establishment of the United Nations Counterterrorism Center, UNCT, providing a total of $110 million to support member states and enhance their ability to implement the UN Global Counterterrorism Strategy. We continue to support international effort by actively participating in the Global Counterterrorism Forum the Global Coalition to Defeat Daesh, and the Islamic Military Counterterrorism Coalition, guided by our belief that counterterrorism is a collective responsibility that requires effective partnerships and continuous expertise and knowledge exchange. On extremism prevention, we established the Global Center for Combating Extreme Extremist Ideology at IDEL. The center works to monitor, analyze, and combat extremist discourse and harness modern technology to raise awareness and counter terrorist propaganda in the digital space. Ladies and gentlemen, we believe that capacity building programs must be based on the needs and national priorities of the beneficiary states. These programs must be implemented at the request of and in full coordination with the beneficiary states to ensure sustainability and effectiveness. For example, in Yemen, capacity building is particularly important to counter the growing threat of terrorist groups, including the terrorist Houthi militia and al Qaeda, seeking to access and exploit modern technologies such as drones and other emerging technologies. In this regard, through the Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen, in coordination with the legitimate Yemeni government, we have supported effort to build the capacities of Yemeni security institutions to counter terrorism, especially in liberated regions in southern Yemen. Detect and disrupt financial and logistical support networks, and stop attempts to transfer technology and military capabilities to terrorist groups. This contributes to bolstering security and stability and prevents these groups from exploiting security vacuum to expand their activities. To conclude, countering the misuse of new technologies by terrorist groups requires that we strengthen international cooperation, exchange expertise, and invest in capacity building so these technologies are harnessed to benefit security, development, and prosperity, not exploited to spread violence and extremism. I thank you.

Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, it is a pleasure, real pleasure to co-chair with His Excellency Dr. Abdulaziz Al-Wassi, Permanent Representative of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, this important session on strategic capacity building to counter the misuse of artificial intelligence. And emerging technologies. Today's discussion comes at a critical moment. Rapid technological innovation is fundamentally reshaping the global counterterrorism landscape. Violent extremist groups are increasingly exploiting AI, digital platforms, cyber capacity— uh, capabilities, unmanned systems, and encrypted communications to advance recruitment, radicalization, financing, operational planning, and attacks themselves. These tools are lowering barriers to entry, expanding reach, and accelerating the speed at which threatens threats can materialize. The 2024 Global Index on Responsible AI found that 92 countries out of 138, almost 6 billion people, live without adequate protection from AI-related risks. At the same time, these technologies offer great promises for accelerating development and inclusion. They can strengthen early warning systems, support prevention efforts, and enhance more effective and targeted responses. The dual-use nature of AI, where innovation creates both opportunity and risk, makes this one of the most dynamic and complex dimensions of contemporary counter-terrorism. For UNDP, this underscores the importance of a prevention-oriented and capacity-driven approach. This means taking proactive efforts to counter discrimination, disinformation, strengthen digital literacy, and protect the integrity of information ecosystems. Especially at the community level. Our role as UNDP is to support member states in strengthening governance systems, building resilient institutions, and ensuring that digital transformation is inclusive, rights-based, and aligned with the rule of law. No single actor can respond to these challenges alone. Effective solutions require very strong collaboration across governments, across private sector, civil society, and UN system ourselves. We must work together to close capacity gaps, strengthen regulatory frameworks, and ensure that innovations serves peace, security, and development. At the UNDP's workshops, community-led action by youth, journalists, and local peacebuilders can transform online spaces into platforms of trust, inclusion, and prevention. This session provides us with an opportunity to move from analysis to action by identifying practical approaches, sharing experience, and forging partnerships that can keep pace with technological change. Reiterating the Secretary-General's remarks on the four priorities—prevention, cooperation, technology, and values—of the UN Counterterrorism Strategy Review, I do look forward to a very rich and forward-looking discussion. Thank you.

Thank you, Assistant Secretary General Ms. Noda. We will now turn to our special guests for their interventions. It is my pleasure to give the floor to Dr. Mohammed Al-Kuwaiti, Head of Cyber Security Council of the United Arab Emiratis.

Chair, executives, excellencies, distinguished guests, thank you very much for allowing me to be a part of this. And let me begin by thanking the co-chair and the organizer for inviting me to participate as a special guest in this important session. I also thank them for bringing us together and for placing artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and emerging technologies at the heart of our discussion. These issues are now really a center to the cybersecurity as well as to security in general of every nation and to the safety security of the people we serve. We meet at a moment of profound transformation. AI and cyberspace are reshaping the environment in which we all operate. They provide governments with powerful new tools to detect threats, protect critical infrastructure, and keep their people safe. Yet these capabilities are also being misused for terrorist purposes and by violent extremist actors, including to spread propaganda at scale, recruit and radicalize, create synthesized media that deceives and incites violence, and operate across borders while seeking to evade detection. The challenges before us is to ensure that these technologies remain instruments for justice and security and never become weapons in the land or in the hand of these who seek to do harm. This is why our shared task is to keep cyberspace safe and secure and to ensure that artificial intelligence is developed and used in ways that are safe, secure, and trustworthy. Technology is advancing faster than the institutions many of us serve. Our responsibility, therefore, is not simply to acquire new tools. It is to ensure that our institutions, our cyber capabilities, and our decision-making evolves as quickly as technology itself. The experience of the United Arab Emirates has taught us one lesson above all. In cybersecurity and in artificial intelligence, technology alone is not enough. A safe and secure digital environment does not come from system and software alone. It depends on strong institutions, skilled and trusted people, secure and well-governed data, resilient cybersecurity, clear governance, and effective cooperation Coordination, partnership across entities and agencies. Where these foundations are in place, AI and cyber capabilities become a genuine advantage. Where they are absent, even the most advanced systems will fall short and may themselves become a point of vulnerability. We have also learned that readiness in this field is not a destination, but a continuous process. Cyber threats that accompany it evolves just as quickly. Institutions must therefore learn to adapt continuously, remain agile, learn as they go, adapt to new technologies responsibly, and keep their systems secure as threats evolve. Building institutions that adopt by habit rather than by exception is perhaps the defining capacity-building challenge of our time. This leads me to a reflection drawn directly from our national experience. In countering the misuse of AI and emerging technologies, the most valuable form of capacity-building is not the transfer of technology, but the development of lasting sovereign capability knowledge, and expertise. We can support one another by sharing operation experience and the lessons we have learned, by building technical partnership, investing in people and in cybersecurity workforce, and strengthening national cyber and digital resiliency. Our aim should be to build enduring institutional capacity and digital space that remains safe and secure, rather than simply acquiring systems that may quickly become obsolete. None of this can be achieved by any country acting alone. In cyberspace, those who misuse these technologies respect no borders. Our response must be equal, collaborative, and transnational, guided by the rule of law, Government, the United Nations, industry, and academia each have an essential part to play in sharing expertise, supporting national capacity building, building trusted partnership, and ensuring that artificial intelligence and cyber capabilities strengthen justice and security in accordance with international law, including our respective obligations under international human rights low. The United Arab Emirates is fully committed to this shared endeavor. We believe that with the right foundations, the right partnership, and a steady commitment to responsible innovation, artificial intelligence, and safe and secure cyberspace can serve the very purpose that brings us together here today: to protect our nations from terrorism, and to safeguard the security and the dignity of the people we are here to serve. I thank you very much for allowing me to be a part of this and looking forward for more discussion. Thank you very much.

I would like to thank Dr. Al-Kuwaiti for your valuable remarks. It's now my pleasure to give the floor to Mr. Amandeep Singh Gill, Under-Secretary-General and Special Envoy for Digital and Emerging Technologies.

Excellency, distinguished colleagues, thank you very much for this opportunity to share some Thank you, Mr. Kharif, for your thoughts. The question we are addressing today, strategic capacity building in countering the misuse of new and emerging technologies, is most timely. It's really at the heart of the challenge we face from the misuse of these very powerful technologies. We are not building the right capacities fast enough., in response to these rapid developments. And this is something that I really want to bring home to you, uh, today. The threats, the risks that we are seeing with these technologies are no longer theoretical. Uh, very recently, a powerful AI model, uh, was used to discover thousands of cybersecurity vulnerabilities, uh, that lay out there in some platforms that have thousands of people looking at them over years. So these capabilities are enormously powerful today, and in the wrong hands, they can wreak a lot of effort. There is the side of enabling and amplification. So emerging technologies and AI are already being leveraged to amplify propaganda, scale recruitment and automate targeting with a scale and speed never seen before. So the response also has to scale up and speed up. I think the larger challenge, the more profound challenges, is the speed of change. Every day, every week, new models, new harnesses for those models, new applications. So institutions that have been— used to a more slow pace of change are struggling to keep up. This is a structural gap that we must address because in counterterrorism, this structural gap translates directly into risk to people, to communities, and to frontline institutions. So what we need to do is approach strategic capacity building not as a long-term objective, as an immediate necessity. At the United Nations, momentum has been building up on artificial intelligence pursuant to the agreement in 2024 on the Global Digital Compact, which called for stronger AI capacity-building partnerships and a more coordinated approach to global digital cooperation. Last year, in 2025, that commitment was translated into concrete mechanisms, the independent international scientific panel and the global dialogue on AI governance, as well as the thinking, the options presented by the Secretary-General in his report on innovative voluntary financing options for AI capacity building, including the goal of helping countries reach a minimum irreducible AI capacity. This year, member states are taking clear, tangible steps. The report of the scientific panel is due tomorrow. It will be available just before the dialogue next week in Geneva, and you will see in the report examples of how powerful the impact is and what is the pace of development and how it is posing new challenges in terms of responding to the non-state actor threat, whether it's the lift in, um, bioweapons-related capacity or cybersecurity, um, offensive capacity. In parallel, member states are taking steps through a voluntary AI capacity development network, a member-state-led platform designed to foster collaboration and knowledge sharing across the various aspects of AI, from data and compute to skills and technical advisory support. We need to be clear that these efforts are not just about tools or technology. They are about people and systems, the ability of institutions to absorb rapid change, to understand this change, the ability of practitioners to interpret new risks, and the ability of governments everywhere to act with with confidence in an increasingly complex digital environment. In this, for us at the United Nations, it's a cardinal principle that we should adopt a human-centered approach. It's not an abstract principle. In the context of counterterrorism, it means asking very concrete questions like who's being exposed, targeted, or exploited? Who's left without access to support or protection, and how can these same technologies be used to restore agency and dignity. In this regard, I commend the work of UN OCT on the gap analysis of digital tools to support victims of terrorism. It reminds us that digital innovation must not only counter threats, it must also serve those who have been most directly affected by them. Let me conclude. With one reflection. If technological change continues to accelerate, and it will, then our collective response must also accelerate, not only in terms of tools but in terms of trust, coordination, and shared capacity, because without stronger cooperation, the misuse of these technologies will continue to outpace us. With the right investments in people, in institutions, and in international cooperation, we will have the opportunity to ensure that emerging technologies are not a vector of harm but a tool for protection, resilience, and ultimately prevention. I thank you.

I thank— I thank Mr. Gill for his remarks. And we will now turn to our distinguished panelists. But before doing so, I appeal to all speakers to observe time, at least in line with the UN80 initiative and the efficiency, but as well as to face the challenge of long list of speakers, and we have to finish on time. Now I invite His Excellency Mr. Song Yu, Deputy Permanent Representative of the People's Republic of China to the United Nations, to take the floor.

Ambassador Alwassol, Assistant Secretary-General Shoko Noda, colleagues. This year marks The 20th anniversary of the adoption of the UN Global Counterterrorism Strategy. This high-level meeting is very timely and is of great significance for raising global awareness and strengthening international counterterrorism synergy. I thank the co-chairs as well as the special guests for the important addresses just made. Against the In the current global counter-terrorism backdrop that remains grim, terrorist activities are increasingly intertwined with geopolitical conflicts, while terrorist forces step up the use of emerging technologies such as new media, drones, and artificial intelligence, making their operations ever more covert and destructive. At the same time, international counter-terrorism efforts are becoming politicized, bloc-based, and instrumentalized, With certain countries adopting selective approaches to fighting terrorism, thus undermining the foundation of international cooperation. On strengthening international counterterrorism cooperation, I wish to make 4 proposals. First, uphold the right principles and build synergy in fighting terrorism. Countries should stay committed to a new vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative, and sustainable security. Strengthen the UN's central coordinating role in international counterterrorism cooperation. Resolutely combat all terrorist organizations and individuals listed by the Security Council and oppose selective approaches and double standards. We must firmly oppose groundlessly attacking or discrediting other countries' legitimate counterterrorism and de-radicalization measures and interfering in others' internal affairs under the pretext of human rights, ethnicity, or religion. Second, adopt comprehensive approaches and eliminate the root causes of terrorism. The rise of terrorism is often a product of regional conflicts. We must promote political solutions to hotspot issues to deny terrorist forces opportunities to exploit instability. Underdevelopment is a key driver behind the persistence of terrorism. Support should be given to developing countries to improve livelihoods, eradicate poverty, and accelerate implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development in a bid to break the vicious cycle of poverty begetting terrorism. Third, strengthen capacity building and enhance effectiveness of counterterrorism efforts. Developing countries face dual challenges of insufficient capacity and inadequate resources in fighting terrorism. In keeping with the problems identified in fighting terrorism and the countries' technical assistance needs, constructive assistance should be provided in keeping with national specificities. Global counterterrorism resources should be further directed towards developed countries, especially those facing higher risks, to effectively strengthen their capabilities. Fourth, enhance governance of technology and respond to emerging threats. China supports the implementation of the Abu Dhabi Guiding Principles and encourages all countries to incorporate drone-based terrorist attacks into national counter-terrorism strategies and risk assessments while strengthening legal regulation risk assessment, and capacity building in taking countermeasures. Efforts should be made to actively promote training and infrastructure development for AI-based counterterrorism, enhancing member states' ability to leverage AI to prevent and combat terrorism. At the same time, the legitimate civilian use and innovation of emerging technologies must also be safeguarded, so as to ensure a balance between counterterrorism security needs and lawful technological applications. Colleagues. In response to threats posed by terrorist forces such as ETRM, China has developed a counterterrorism approach that combines suppression with prevention, with notable results in fighting terrorism in accordance with the law. As a determined participant in and active contributor to international counterterrorism cooperation, China actively implements the Global Counterterrorism Strategy, shares its successful experience in counterterrorism, and direct— direct internationalization and supports capacity building in relevant countries. President Xi Jinping's Global Security Initiative and Global Governance Initiative provide important guidance for strengthening international counterterrorism cooperation. China stands ready to work with all parties to build up consensus, enhance coordinated action, and contribute more to building a future free from terrorism. I thank you.

I thank His Excellency Mr. Son Yu for his remarks. I now invite His Excellency Mr. Hiroyuki Minami, Ambassador in Charge of International Cooperation for Counterterrorism and International Organized Crime of Japan, to take the floor. Ambassador Minami will speak from the lectern.

Thank you, co-chair. Thank you very much, chair. I would like to express my respect for the daily dedication of many UN officials, representatives from various countries, those in academia and the private sector, and all the other people involved. I would also like to thank you for all the preparation you have made for today's Welcome to the conference. Today I am honored to have been given the opportunity to speak at such an important forum. The theme of today's— yesterday's, today's end conference is "A Future Free from Terrorism." When we consider what terrorism is, it is said alongside with genocide, it is one of the most difficult concepts to define. I have been involved in work within my government dealing with international terrorism for 2.5 years, and most of the multilateral forums dealing with terrorism I experienced have their roots in the 9/11. The 9/11, which occurred exactly 25 years ago, near here at the Pentagon and on the plains of Pennsylvania, remains the framework of our discussions. On the other hand, looking back at a quarter of a century of history, the environment surrounding terrorism has dramatically changed conceptually and geographically. A quarter of a century ago, we were fighting the same battle against terrorism. Our belief that we must fight terrorism remains unchanged. But as international criminal organizations become more vicious and violent and their vandalism has grown into something that could be called terrorism, and as the concept of international terrorism spreads, the areas where terrorism operates has expanded geographically. Now, international conflicts show no sign of decreasing, the fight against terrorism continues to intensify, and it seems that a future without terrorism may be impossible. However, beyond the conceptual expansion of terrorism and the resulting increase in geographical scope of terrorist activities, a more significant change is occurring. It is exactly about the technology that terrorists misuses in their acts of violence. Their technology is rapidly evolving. As an aside, I believe the reason UNODC is introducing the concept of the Connect Project in tomorrow's side event is because traditional terrorist organizations and newly emerging international organized crime groups that have grown larger and more violent. Both are using similar fundraising methods and employing similar technologies to torment humanity. And it is to show that we must engage in an all-out war to counter the new Axis of Evil. Ladies and gentlemen, according to the UN concept paper, The theme of this meeting is how to address terrorism using new technologies such as AI, drones, and cybersecurity. Only 3 examples have been raised. The UN has repeatedly requested Japan to provide capacity-building support to developing countries. However, we should distinguish on one side the technologies Japan has a comparative advantage in, and on the other, technologies it does not even possess, let alone have a comparative advantage in. For example, Japan has excellent technologies in image analysis. Therefore, by extending facial recognition systems to developing nations to improve the accuracy of immigration control in those countries, Japan is contributing to their counterterrorism efforts. This is already being done sufficiently. Japan is always providing educational opportunities for maritime law enforcement capabilities to developing regions. While Japan can help other countries improve some basic national management capabilities, or governance, so to speak, Japan is not in a position to provide assistance in areas such as long-range drones or highly secure communication apps mostly used in combat zones. To reiterate, there are two types of technologies: one, civilian and general-purpose technologies that is useful in our daily lives, and two, technology primarily used by combatants and terrorists wearing camouflage uniform. Japan can contribute in the first case, as we are already doing. We continue to do it in case of necessity. On the other hand, regarding the latter type of technology, it is actually this type of technology that has made exponential progress in recent years. And the reality is that we have no choice but to wait for cooperation from the countries that actually possess such technologies. The technologies used by combatants and terrorists around the world are causing many casualties and posing a major threat to humanity. But there are two types of countries, of course, that actually possess such technologies. One group is countries that possess advanced military technologies, and they are using them for for their proper security, these countries may or could extend a helping hand to developing regions suffering from heinous acts of terrorists. On the other hand, weapon-level technology is linked to each country's national security, which presents a major problem as it makes it difficult to easily provide technological assistance to other countries. The other group of countries have traditionally been called state sponsors of terrorism and in recent years have been able to manipulate not only their own terrorist group but also those acting as proxy within other countries. It is difficult for the international community to expect aid to developing countries from these countries— those countries. And the international community must once again unite and put pressure on state sponsors of terrorism. Some of these countries are even continuing to fire missiles that are more powerful versions of long-range drones. Now, I will conclude my remarks. Well, the actions of the terrorists and the international organized —groups such as gangs that inflict equally horrific damages upon us are becoming increasingly dangerous due to the rapid advancement in the technology they utilize. Some of this high-tech involves the use of civilian general-purpose components and knowledge related to Japan's superior technological capabilities will undoubtedly be useful in global counterterrorism efforts. We are providing assistance and continue. On the other hand, if the drones, AI, cyber technologies described in this conference's concept paper represent the latest military technologies used not only by terrorists but also the soldiers engaged in warfare in conflict zones, then Japan, a peaceful country, lacks knowledge and expertise to provide assistance. Specifically regarding drones, since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, there have been unprecedented technological advancements, and it has been reported that some drones now have operation capabilities comparable to those of certain missile systems. These are military drones, not civilian ones. Technologically advanced countries are pursuing technological innovation to ensure their own country, so it is understandable that providing assistance to a developing country would be difficult. Looking back at our world history, technological innovation has continuously enriched our lives. The military industry is an exception, exception, only exception maybe. If the continuation of war, conflict, skirmish is fueling technological innovation used not only by soldiers but by terrorists, then ending armed conflict would be the greatest aid we can offer to the developing countries. This is a serious challenge for the United Nations and India. For the international community. Thank you for listening.

I would like to thank His Excellency Mr. Minami for his remarks, and I now invite Mr. Kibiego Kigen, the Director General of the National Counterterrorism Centre of the Republic of Kenya. The floor is yours.

Thank you, Co-Chairs, Excellencies, distinguished colleagues. New emerging and disruptive technologies are fundamentally reshaping the way we live, work, and interact. These transformations are felt most acutely in counter-terrorism, where practitioners confront both unprecedented risks and unparalleled opportunities. Artificial intelligence in particular epitomizes this duality. Its velocity, accessibility, and adaptability are transformative and enabling it to serve simultaneously as a force multiplier for state security and hyper-accelerator for asymmetric threats. This dual use means that the very capabilities engineered to enhance national security and social well-being are being repurposed to undermine them. In the hands of national security agencies, artificial intelligence delivers a new leap in capability, enabling the real-time processing of vast streams of intelligence, the automated detection, detection of illicit networks, and the deployment of, of predictive analytics to strengthen early warning systems. Equally, the widespread of artificial intelligence has radically lowered the barrier to entry for asymmetric warfare. Access to AI now enables terrorist actors to exercise state-level influence without the vast industrial, industrial infrastructure once required to achieve strategic impact. The diffusion of capability facilitated by AI has eroded the traditional symmetry between the state and non-state power, allowing extremists to project strategic influence by leveraging algorithmic precision, digital anonymity, and global connectivity at, at, at, at, at unprecedented speed and scale. As a result, the strategic burden has shifted for counterterrorism practitioners. Security today is increasingly defined by the capability— capacity to sustain a technological edge in an environment where algorithms evolve faster than institutions can adapt. The contest is now one of agility over inertia, innovation over convention, and foresight over reaction. To prevail, practitioners must not only master the tools of the present but also anticipate future trajectories and ensure that policy frameworks keep pace with the velocity of technological disruption. This changing environment compels counterterrorism practitioners to abandon a traditional reactive posture and embrace a proactive, technologically agile strategy. The decisive advantage lies in leveraging innovation to outpace adversaries, embedding resilience into systems, and ensuring policy frameworks evolve in step with the velocity of disruption. In this context, foresight is the ultimate, ultimate safeguard, agility the defining strength, and adaptability the enduring measures of success. Distinguished colleagues, as we embrace the opportunities of artificial intelligence, we must strike the right balance. We should avoid regulating innovation out of fear, but should ensure that AI is always used within the rule of law, with respect for human rights. Innovation and security should strengthen one another, not come at each other's expense. Using AI without accountability or legal oversight risks undermining the values we seek to protect. Our responsibility is to ensure that AI is developed and used responsibly, guided by legality, ethics, transparency, and respect for fundamental rights. Ladies and gentlemen, artificial intelligence is a shared global resource, and protecting it is a shared responsibility. By working together, we can harness its benefits to strengthen security while preventing its exploitation by terrorists. Through cooperation, responsible innovation, and vigilance, we can ensure that technology remains a force for peace security, and the common good. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Mr. Kigam, for your remarks. Now I would like to invite Mr. Wonho Park, the head of the National Counterterrorism Center of the Prime Minister's Office of the Republic of Korea. The floor is yours.

Thank you very much. Distinguished co-chairs, esteemed UNOCT colleagues, and delegates from around the world. It is a great honor to represent the Republic of Korea and speak before you today. My name is Wonho Park, Administrator of the Korea National Counterterrorism Center. The National Counterterrorism Center was established in 2016 following the enactment of the Act on Anti-Terrorism for the Protection of Citizens and Public Security. Since then, the Center has served as the main body overseeing and coordinating all national counterterrorism policies and operations. Marking our 10th anniversary this year. To meet the rapidly changing security and terror environment, our center is driving a complete innovation of the national counterterrorism system. One of the primary objectives of this reform is to proactively counter the compounding threat of modern terrorism fueled by advanced technologies. Such as drones, unmanned systems, cyber operations, and artificial intelligence, the very topic we are discussing today. Amid global instability, terrorist incidents continue without pause, threatening the daily lives of everyone here. My country, Korea, is no exception. Ko Chairs and distinguished delegates, while we marvel at generative AI and its bright future, this technology has become a new challenge, hacking the most vulnerable part of humanity, our heart and mind. When copying someone's voice with just a few seconds of data for crime is possible. AI terror is no longer a distant future, but a threat that could strike tomorrow or even today. Similarly, while we cheer for the innovation and convenience of drones, these small aircraft, aircraft have become a real security threat, penetrating the blind spot where our advanced radar network cannot reach. Drone-based terror, where a hard-to-detect aircraft flies freely over clouded cities, strikes major facilities, and paralyzes the entire systems. Is no longer a matter of if, but when and where. In response, the Korean government has recently established the National AI Security Center to systematically and effectively counter emerging cybersecurity threats driven by artificial intelligence. Through this center, we are building a comprehensive AI security guidebook and risk management frameworks to lead the responsible and safe use of AI technology. In addition to this action, the Republic of Korea plans to launch the National Drone and Counter-Drone Strategy Task Force directly under the Prime Minister's Office to establish a powerful pan-government control tower. Through this framework, we will invest significant budget over the next 5 years to build advanced integrated counter-drone defense systems for critical national facilities and drive technical standardization. However, the asymmetric fear of technologies escaping human control and threatening our cities cannot be solved by one nation alone. It demands united global response. It is in this context that the National Counterterrorism Center of the Republic of Korea strongly supports and actively joins the global coalition to counter and eradicate terrorism. While joining international efforts, we plan to expand bilateral exchanges with UN member states, specifically, We wish to institutionalize cooperation by signing MOUs with counterpart agencies that oversee national counterterrorism action worldwide, solving our common problems through common efforts. Terrorism seeks to divide us. However, our unity will deep it in. I thank you.

I thank Mr. Park for his remarks, and before giving the floor to the next panelist, I would like just to remind the speakers of the time, as we are already behind. I now give the floor Mr. François-Javier Martin Lazarega, Director of the Center for Intelligence Against Terrorism and Organized Crimes of Spain. Excellency, you have the floor.

Dear colleagues, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, thank you very much for the introduction. It's an honor for me to be here with all of you. Now, we can also— we can all agree that terrorism and extremist movements have found in artificial intelligence and in technology something that would magnify the impact of their actions. We have spoken a great deal about how AI being used for terrorist purposes includes automated attacks with drones, the use of malware to attack critical infrastructure, as well as designing biological and chemical threats, which is beyond scientific oversight. And the misuse of AI makes it possible to alter recommended algorithms of digital platforms. It allows terrorist propaganda. As well as massive disinformation operations. And all this through the use of decentralized finances, cryptocurrency, and complex transactions on the dark web, which make it difficult to trace these monetary flows. Yes, we've spoken about how the new technologies are a fundamental tool in order to protect critical infrastructure and public spaces, or how the counterterrorist response has greatly increased our data processing capability and predictive analysis to identify financing patterns, to locate propaganda in real time, as well as structured hate speech. Now, we cannot consider artificial intelligence as an instrument which terrorists use to attack and for the state to use to defend itself. We find ourselves before a transformative technology which alters all of society, which is reconfiguring in a swift fashion institutions, labor markets, and personal relations. We find ourselves before a hyper-technification, if you like, which could generate conditions of grievance, alienation, discontent, like the ones that historically preceded outbreaks of violence, political violence, and violent extremism. Now, when we automate administrative decisions that have an impact on the rights of people, even though we gain in terms of time and objectivity, We are avoiding having an identifiable human agent who could assume responsibility for these decisions. This accountability gap deprives institutions of their legitimacy and plunges citizens in a sort of defenseless existence when they perceive that their lives are governed by machines. This resentment is sharpened when, in automatic decisions. We see discriminatory biases that reproduce injustice towards vulnerable sectors in the labor sphere. This new technology could create and is creating large numbers of displaced workers. But unlike previous economic revolutions, this transformation doesn't only replace physical labor, but it's also dismantling intellectual, administrative, and creative professions of broad sectors of society, thus, uh, creating fertile ground for extremist recruitment. And furthermore, the dizzying pace of AI clashes with the institutional time lag. Uh, the, uh, uh, innovation cycle of, uh, uh, technological corporations moves in weeks, whereas, uh, administrative, administrative decisions or international treaties take years to be produced. This This state paralysis accelerates this perception of what could be a capture of the state by corporations. If AI computers and infrastructures are controlled by a handful of— handful of private transnational companies, the real sovereignty could go beyond democratic control. Furthermore, the massive implementation of biometrics Indiscriminate facial recognition or automatic identification in public spaces, even though it can be justified to fight terrorism, it could undermine privacy as well as other fundamental rights. And that is why, along with classic conventional terrorism, we must be vigilant when it comes to the development of extremism, which are based on this anti-technological accelerationism. And in the 19th century, after the Industrial Revolution in Europe, the Luddite movement brought together textile workers whose lives were threatened, and they destroyed mechanical looms. The current neo-Luddism is made up of philosophers, ecologists, and well-educated intellectuals that see in AI an existential threat for the human condition. Mitigation strategies vis-à-vis these threats, whether they're terrorist or not, cannot be limited to simply the security sphere.— close cooperation between countries and their agencies. We have to opt for public and private governance through multilateral frameworks such as the European Union Internet Forum or the GIFCT, which apply coercive tools which require that technological companies remove violent content. Quickly. Beyond this, the network could neutralize content before it becomes viral and develop counter-narrative campaigns in real time. So when users are doing searches and looking for extremist content, their attention would be diverted automatically towards alternative content such as the testimonies of victims of terrorism or psychosocial support resources. This prevention strategy, especially starting with the, uh, the youth, can find in gaming a resource with the design of educational role-playing designed to promote critical capability as well as learning about disinformation and media manipulation. The accountability gap must be resolved with the principle of the man in the loop. And forbidding automation of any decision that would affect the rights, the freedom, and lives of people, guaranteeing that a human supervisor would assume the civil, penal, and ethical responsibility of any algorithmic result. And lastly, it's a matter of priority to set up bias audits and oversight of recommended algorithms to change or alter functions that contain polarizing content and to ensure that they don't amplify radical discourse. At the same time, we have to look at explainable artificial intelligence to prevent counterterrorism models from operating as inscrutable black boxes and could be out of control. Their processes should be understandable and auditable, and this is very important. They should make it possible to have the full conversion of their findings into judicial evidence which is robust and which respects guarantees of due process. And I'd like to conclude by saying that technological capacities should be subordinated ethically to unconditional respect for human rights. And the encyclical Magnificat Humanitatis by Pope Leo XIV said that the concentration of technical power escapes the sovereign control of states and weakening governance, creating an environment which is hostile to people. And so he makes an urgent plea to disarm artificial intelligence, intelligence to prevent the technology from having dominion over the human and to place technology at the service of the human family. Thank you very much.

Thank you very much, Mr. Lizarraga. I now would like to invite Mr. Eldor Aripov, First Deputy Head of the Security Council of the Republic of Uzbekistan. The floor is yours, and I hope you can limit your intervention to 5 minutes if possible.

Thank you. Thank you. Dr. Abdulaziz Al-Wazir, Ms. Shoka Noda, Excellencies, distinguished delegates and participants, on behalf of the delegation of the Republic of Uzbekistan, let me express our sincere appreciation to the United Nations Office of Counter-Terrorism for organizing this discussion on a topic of such a strategic importance. Today we stand on the threshold— of unprecedented technological transformation. And as previous speakers already mentioned, artificial intelligence, machine learning, biotechnology, and unmanned systems offer enormous opportunities for sustainable development and for addressing global challenges. At the same time, we must acknowledge— a sobering reality. Terrorist groups are rapidly adding these very technologies to their arsenal. We are witnessing artificial intelligence algorithms being exploited to mass-produce propaganda, generate deepfakes, automated cyberattacks, and recruit the most vulnerable segments of our society. Our youth. Over the past year, the volume of destructive AI-generated content identified by law enforcement agencies in Uzbekistan has doubled. More than 100 extremist publications created with the use of AI are being blocked every day, demonstrating the scale of this emerging threat. The adoption of artificial intelligence has reduced the operational cost of terrorist groups by 80%. At the same time, hosting providers and platforms delete only 30% of all identified terrorist content. Without the consolidation of our collective efforts in this area, we will not be able to counter the informational offensives of our terrorists effectively. Given the rapid pace of digital development, there is a growing trend of using crypto-assets and finance terrorist activities, which necessitates intensified efforts to monitor and analyze suspicious financial transactions. With the support of the Financial Action Task Force and the United Nations Counterterrorism Committee Executive Directorate, we have established an effective mechanism to formalize the information obtained and admit IT as evidence in pre-trial investigations in judicial proceedings. As a result, we have initiated more than 20 criminal cases over the past 3 years alone. Terrorism knows no borders, and in the digital environment such borders do not exist at all. Under these circumstances, traditional response methods are losing their effectiveness. We need preventive action and a strategic strengthening of our defense capacity. Dear colleagues, the Republic of Uzbekistan regards digital security as an integral element of national and regional stability in Central Asia. Within the framework of the national program Digital Uzbekistan 2030 and the strategy for the development of artificial intelligence technologies, our goal is not only to scale up the IT sector but also to build a reliable legal and ethical safeguard. Our approach to countering high-tech terrorism rests on three key pillars. Firstly, the proactive strengthening of the human and technical capacity of law enforcement agencies. Only more advanced technology can effectively counter technology itself. In this regard, in 2025, Uzbekistan adopted a strategic Presidential decree on the digital transformation of the internal affairs system. This initiative aims to implement advanced tools to ensure the safety of citizens and the state. We're actively complementing this new technological foundation by investing in human capital. Law enforcement officers in Uzbekistan are currently undergoing specialized training in cybersecurity. Secondly, the development of an ethical and legal framework geared toward the protection of human rights. In preventing the misuse of AI, we must not infringe upon the fundamental rights and freedoms of our citizens. Uzbekistan is working to introduce artificial intelligence standards that minimize algorithmic bias and guarantee the protection of personal data. Thirdly, inclusive international cooperation and public-private partnership. We need the expertise and the social responsibility of the big tech companies. We have a shared duty to make the global network safer and more trustworthy. In this regard, Uzbekistan proposes the following practical steps: First, establish under the auspices of the United Nations

Sorry, if I may thank you for your remarks, Mr.

Aripov. Because of the time, I think we would like to move on to the next speaker. Now we'd like to invite Mr. Chalok Abyani, Under-Secretary-General and Special Adviser of the Secretary-General on the Prevention of Genocide. The floor is yours.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, I'm honored to join you in today's session alongside distinguished delegates and colleagues convened as part of the 4th High-Level Conference on Counterterrorism. And united in our shared commitment to advancing global efforts against international crimes. I would like to start by thanking the co-chairs of this panel, His Excellency Dr. Abdulaziz M. Alwasi, Permanent Representative of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to the United Nations, and Ms. Shoko Noda, Assistant Secretary-General and Assistant Administrator, Director of the Crisis Bureau of the United Nations Development Programme. I would also like to appreciate and thank my co-panelists for their insights, for their remarks on issues of relevance to all of us. Today's discussion, focusing on the misuse of artificial intelligence and new and emerging technologies, and on our collective responses to these evolving challenges, lies very close to the heart of my mandate as the UN Special Adviser on the Prevention of Genocide including my office's role as the UN system focal point for the implementation of the UN strategy and plan of action on hate speech. Throughout history, from the Holocaust to Rwanda and Srebrenica, hate speech and incitement to discrimination, hostility, or violence have served as big triggers and precursors to the commission of the heinous crime of genocide and of other other atrocity crimes. These tragedies remind us that words, when left unchecked, can deepen divisions, fuel intolerance and exclusion, and in the most serious cases, may even create conditions whereby atrocity crimes become possible or direct in their commission. Today, the internet, social media platforms, together rapidly evolving technologies, Generative AI and other AI-enabled tools, advanced deepfakes and bots, are transforming our information environment and reshaping our societies. While offering enormous opportunities, they also contribute to the spread of hateful narratives targeting groups at risk at unprecedented scale and speed, shaping how people access information and amplify the credibility and visibility of narratives that promote grievances across the world. This is having a profound and very serious and concerning impact offline. Generative AI is now fully equipped to create hyper-realistic content such as images, videos, and audio using just a few existing options or clips, nearly indistinguishable from reality. We have seen already how digital platforms can be exploited to disseminate hate speech and incitement to violence and advance dehumanizing campaigns against minorities. Such campaigns can ultimately lead to genocide and other atrocious crimes. We have also seen instances where hate speech, violent extremism, genocide, and terrorism are interlinked. For example, in the context of the genocide perpetrated by ISIL, against the Yazidi minority in Iraq. This is why today, more than ever, it is important to work together, reinforcing and leveraging our respective mandates at the United Nations, while also understanding that the dire reality on the ground requires urgent, timely, and coordinated response. We need to step up our collective efforts to counter and address this phenomenon, and particularly to further understand how the misuse or abuse of AI and other new and emerging technologies change the dynamics towards further erosion of social cohesion, causing harm, exacerbating conflict, while understanding the new spaces for prevention that this field can also offer. We need to help develop systems and tools that are inclusive, ethical, and aligned with human rights standards and human dignity. We need a multifaceted, comprehensive approach, an approach that is built upon strong partnerships and involving the whole of society. The adoption of the Pact of the Future, including the Global Digital Compact, was a pivotal step forward in this direction, calling for enhanced international cooperation for, I quote, safe, secure, and trustworthy emerging technologies, including AI. Member States ought to continue strengthening appropriate regulatory frameworks in line with international human rights law, including freedom of expression. The UN Strategy and Plan of Action on Hate Speech, together with the Rabat Plan of Action, provide valuable guidance for designing and implementing effective strategies to address and counter hate speech. Technology and social media companies must also take responsibility for the systems they build, including by identifying, preventing, mitigating, and redressing harms from the risks their services may pose. Civil society, religious, traditional, community leaders, women, young people, influencers, and local communities all have essential roles to play and must be empowered. Digital education and media literacy are essential components of a comprehensive strategy to counter hateful narratives and building resilience against online hate speech. Building capacity means looking at all actors of society to promote sustainable peace. But none of this is possible if we don't fully understand the problem. Let me conclude by emphasizing the importance of continued up-to-date and in-depth research on the scope, trends, target.

I, I thank you, Mr. Biani, for your insightful remarks, and I now invite participants to watch and listen to a prerecorded video message by Miss Monica Kathina Juma, Under-Secretary-General and Executive Director of the United Nations Office on Drugs and crime.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I am honored to address the 4th United Nations High-Level Counterterrorism Conference session on the misuse of AI and emerging technologies. This discussion comes at a pivotal time for global security. Terrorist groups are increasingly exploiting artificial intelligence, and new technologies to expand the speed, scale, and reach of their propaganda, recruitment, and operations. As this threat landscape evolves, we must recalibrate our responses and equip criminal justice institutions with the tools they need to keep up with this technological shift. This requires sustained investment in national capacities alongside a coordinated multilateral effort across the United Nations counterterrorism apparatus. For more than 25 years now, UNODC has been at the forefront of this effort. We have helped countries strengthen legislative framework and build strong, accountable criminal justice systems so that they are better prepared for emerging threats. We have trained frontline officials on the responsible use of new technologies, ensuring alignment with international law, human rights standards, and accountability. And together with our partners of the United Nations Global Counterterrorism Coordination Compact, we have developed guidance on the use of electronic evidence to strengthen investigations and facilitate information sharing. This work must now be scaled up and adapted to the realities of an increasingly digital and borderless environment. Against this background, the 9th review of the Global Counterterrorism Strategy is a timely opportunity to reinforce our collective commitment commitment. UNODC stands ready to support Member States and our partners in advancing our joint efforts for a world that is safer from the threat of terrorism. I thank you for your attention.

I thank Ms. Jumaa for her message, and I now invite Mr. Mauro Medico, Director for Capacity Building and Director of the United Nations Counter-Terrorism Centre of the United Nations Office of Counter-Terrorism. The floor is yours.

Thank you very much, Ambassador Wazil. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. With the advent of artificial intelligence and other new technologies, we are no longer addressing only digital disruptions of the past decade. We are witnessing a significant shift in the global security landscape. Member States need capacities to respond to this shift. The General Assembly and UN Member States already in 2021, through the 7th Review of the United Nations Global Counter-Terrorist Strategy, called upon UNOCT to support Member States in building their capacities to respond to the challenges and opportunities that new technologies provide in countering terrorism. The UN Counter-Terrorism Centre promptly responded to this call through its Cybersecurity and New Technologies Programme, with the financial support of all of our donors, and in particular the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the European Union, Japan, the United Arab Emirates, the Republic of Korea, and Germany. With our partners, we started to support Member States develop strategic responses to new technologies through their National Counter-Terrorism strategies. We help them to strengthen their law enforcement technological capabilities and to better protect their critical infrastructure from terrorist cyber attacks. There are three things that are essential, in our views, to make capacity building responses strategic. First, always ensure national ownership and a tailored approach. Capacity building on new technologies needs to address individual countries' needs and technological readiness. Nigeria, Ghana, Uzbekistan, the Philippines, and many more countries that UNCCCT has supported can attest our assistance on new technologies, aligned with the national context, helped them advance integration of new technologies in their counter-terrorism efforts. We have done this through strengthened counter-terrorism strategies, new AI legislation and regulation, strengthened law enforcement responses, or improved partnerships with the private sector. Secondly, strategic capacity building on new technologies requires more than just training to counter terrorism agencies and delivery of equipment. Effective capacity building needs to include a whole-of-government and a whole-of-society dialogue and agreement on how to responsibly use new technologies counter-terrorism. Effective capacity building needs to strengthen the governance and oversight frameworks for technological use, especially AI, and improve institutional coordination. The recently launched training for parliamentarians on artificial intelligence and counter-terrorism is addressing all these aspects and has been well accepted by many member states. We have also launched a gap analysis of digital tools to support Victims of Terrorism, with an aim at aligning digital tools with victims' needs to establish a clear path for safe, responsible and victim-centred digital innovation. And thirdly, effective capacity building on new technologies requires partnership and coordination. This is the only way that Member States can build strategic capacities to respond to the challenges and opportunities of new technologies to counter terrorism. Isolated capacity-building efforts on new technologies are likely to fail unless they are part of a broader comprehensive strategy. UNOCT remains committed to working with Member States and our partners to ensure that technological progress strengthens, rather than undermines, our collective efforts to prevent and counter terrorism and protect human rights. Sustaining the commitment requires continued investment. We therefore count on Member States and regional organizations to continue to support the Counter-Terrorism Centre and UNOCT in building Member States' strategic responses to artificial intelligence and other new technologies in countering terrorism. And I thank you.

Thank you very much, Mr. Miedico, for your remarks, and all the panelists. For your excellent contributions. Now we'll open the floor for questions and observations, and we have a number of speakers already lined up. Additional intervention will be taken as time permits, but probably not because we— I think we have a hard end at 4:45. So I would like to kindly remind all the speakers to limit your intervention to 2 minutes. Without further ado, I would like to first give the floor to the first speaker on the list, who is Major General Fanin Ronni Mutize, Director General of the National Counterterrorism Centre, Zimbabwe.

Koachas, distinguished delegates, Zimbabwe expresses her appreciation to the United Nations Secretary-General for convening this 4th High-Level Conference of heads of counter-terrorism agencies of member states, to the United Nations Office of Counter-Terrorism and to all Global Counter-Terrorism Coordination Compact entities, donors and partners for making this conference possible. The review process is critical to reflect on the implementation of the United Nations Global Counterterrorism Strategy and to consider the evolving threat landscape and appropriate responses. Zimbabwe adds her voice to the deep concerns regarding the evolving global terrorism threat landscape, and we take note of the reports of the Secretary-General and the Security Council 1267 Committee, among others. The proliferation of terrorist groups and related non-state armed groups poses a serious threat to international security and to the territorial integrity of several member states. Zimbabwe calls for enhanced exchanges of operational information, including on the actions or movements of terrorist persons or networks, identification of forged or falsified documents, means of communication used by terrorist groups, trafficking in small arms and light weapons, explosives, and sensitive materials. Co-chairs, distinguished delegates, we are concerned about the reported links between terrorist groups and organized crime, as well as the exploitation of natural resources to further their nefarious activities. Terrorist groups use local grievances to subvert some communities and embed their fighters within them. The terrorism threat requires a comprehensive, multidimensional, and multilateral approach focused on the balanced implementation of the Global Counterterrorism Strategy across its four pillars. Capacity building should be provided to support developing countries' effective counterterrorism measures, and in this vein, Zimbabwe calls for the strengthening of cooperation between the United Nations and regional organizations. Co-chairs, distinguished delegates, as we continue to engage in this review process, Zimbabwe assures you of its constructive engagement. I thank you.
I thank you, Major General Motsirihi, for your remarks, and I now give the floor to Mr. Idris Munir Lallili, Acting Director, African Union Commission.

Thank you, Chair.

Speaking on behalf of the African Union, I wish to share both how we read the evolving threat and above all what Africa is doing about it. Excellencies, Africa today carries a disproportionate share of the global terrorism burden. Between 70 to 75% of terrorism-related deaths are registered in Africa. The Sahel remains the epicenter while the threat continues to expand its footprint and consolidating its presence along the Sahel, West Africa, the Lake Chad basins, the Horn and Central Africa, and parts of Southern Africa region, while spreading its tentacles towards coastal West Africa. Indeed, as we speak today, terrorist groups are occupying and administering an accumulative area of approximately 900,000 square kilometers, roughly the size of Tanzania. The nature of the threat is also changing. In several theaters, these groups no longer operate merely as armed actors. They are increasingly replacing the states as the de facto authority, increasing— governing, sorry, territories and governing populations while exploiting illegal economies and transnational criminal networks. They also are leveraging and continue to leverage drones, encrypted communications, digital finances, and artificial intelligence to enhance their capabilities. At the same time, we are witnessing an alarming privatization of both security and insecurity with the growing use of private military companies, mercenaries, foreign fighters, and seasonal fighters that are recruited locally, regionally, and beyond. The threats transcend borders through arms proliferation, displacement, terrorist mobility. Its adaptation cycle is measured in weeks, while our responses, unfortunately, are still measured in months, if not years. This is why our collective response must be equally agile, coordinated, anticipatory, and sustained. Having said that, Africa has not remained idle or a passive observer of this threat. Through our institution, we are delivering concrete African member states' responses across the continent. For the sake of time, I'll simply invite you to a side event that we will be organizing on the 2nd of July at 10 o'clock. The efforts themselves are anchored In the African Union Comprehensive Counterterrorism Plan of Action that we are rolling out, 2026-2030, being advanced through the AU Peace and Security Council, it provides a common African framework to align national, regional, and continental efforts, strengthen early warning and early action, disrupt terrorist financing and criminal networks, and keep counterterrorism firmly anchored in human rights, and rule of law. The Continental Plan of Action is guided by the principles of African ownership, national responsibilities, regional solidarity, sustainable capacity building, prevention inclusion, evidence-based decision-making, and strengthened international partnership aligned with African priorities. Excellencies, to conclude, Africa stands ready to contribute a more effective global counterterrorism architecture, not as passive recipients of assistance, but as partners that bring analysis, 20 years of experience and expertise, institutional and operational lessons. The threat is changing. Africa is also changing with it and how it approaches the threat of terrorism, and it will require the support and better coordinated efforts from our international partners intervening on the African continent. I thank you for your attention.
Thank you very much, Mr. Lalali. Now I would like to invite His Excellency, Mr. Kholi Sack, Permanent Representative of Senegal to the United Nations. The floor is yours. Je vous remercie.

Thank you.

Thank you, Madam Chair, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. Senegal is pleased to be taking the floor at this meeting on the developments of the global terrorist threat. Terrorism is no longer localized. It's become a transnational system which is interconnected, and it's fueled by poverty, organized crime, illicit financial flows, and the diversion of ITCs and artificial intelligence. Given these changes, our response needs to be comprehensive, coordinated, and anticipatory. In this regard, the Global United Nations Counterterrorism Strategy— and we're celebrating the 20th year anniversary of that— must remain our major framework. We hail the work of the United Nations Office of Counterterrorism, as well as the Global Compact, which are strengthening the coherence of UN work. Africa, especially Sahel, is one of the epicenters of this threat. This reality shows that the security of every one of our states is contingent on the security of its neighbors. This is why bolstering the capacity of Africa remains an imperative. That means we need predictable, sustainable financing. We need well-adapted teams, and we need better sharing of intelligence, and we need African Peace and Security Initiatives as well. But we also know that no exclusively security response can sustainably beat terrorism. Security needs to be coupled with development, with community resilience, and with the integration of young people in the prevention of violent extremism. This is precisely what Senegal has chosen, which has implemented a holistic approach. It's grounded in prevention, the resilience of the populations, the involvement of young people and women, inter alia. In closing, the combat against terrorism is a matter of international solidarity. It requires more preparation, more trust, and more shared responsibility. In pooling our efforts, we can craft a world where security, development, and human dignity will be mutually reinforcing and where victims will find justice, reparations, and hope. Fighting terrorism must be collective or it will not happen.
Thank you. Thank you, Ambassador Szeged, for your remarks. I now give the floor to Ms. Katalin Takácsy, Counterterrorism Expert, Permanent Mission of Hungary to the United Nations.

Thank you, Mr. Co-chair. Please allow me to deliver the following statement on behalf of Her Excellency Ambassador Horváth, as after her work negotiation, she is currently at the UN Peacekeeping Operation Budget Adoption as the chair of the First Committee. Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, Hungary welcomes this timely discussion on technology and— global security. 3 years ago, during Counterterrorism Week in 2023, we were already discussing the implications of emerging technologies. Since then, however, the landscape has changed dramatically. Terrorist organizations have become increasingly adaptive, exploiting a growing number of digital platforms to spread propaganda, recruit supporters, raise funds, and coordinate their activities. Activities. Recent international assessments indicate that extremist networks now operate across more than 150 online platforms simultaneously. Young people remain particularly vulnerable to these rapidly evolving digital threats. Technology therefore presents us with a dual challenge. It creates new opportunities for terrorists, but at the same time providing us with powerful tools to strengthen our response. In this complex environment, artificial intelligence is no longer a technology of the future. It has become a strategic necessity for effective counterterrorism efforts. AI enables authorities and online platforms to detect, identify, and remove terrorist contact at the scale and speed that would be impossible through human effort alone. By analyzing text, images, videos, and behavioral patterns, AI can significantly reduce the time during which extremist content remains accessible online, thereby limiting its reach and impact. Beyond content moderation, AI can also help identify patterns of offline radicalization by analyzing behavioral indicators and network connections. It can support the early identification of individuals who may be vulnerable to extremist influence. This allows member states to complement reactive measures with targeted preventive actions, including credible counter-narratives and early intervention initiatives. At the same time, we must recognize that artificial intelligence is a tool, not a substitute for human judgment. Its deployment must remain firmly anchored in— in respect for human rights, the rule of law, transparency, and appropriate human oversight. Mr. Kocher— Kocher, no country can address these challenges alone. Effective responses require closer international cooperation, the exchange of lessons learned and the best practices, and continued collaboration among governments, international organizations, the private sector, and the academia. In conclusion, artificial intelligence offers unprecedented opportunities to strengthen our collective efforts against terrorism. It enables us to move beyond reacting to terrorist activity towards preventing it, disrupting extremist networks before they can cause harm, and better protecting our societies. By combining technical innovation with responsible governance and international cooperation, we can ensure that emerging technologies remain a force for security rather than a tool for those who seek to undermine it. I thank you.
Thank you very much, Ms. Takács. Now I would like to invite a representative of the Permanent Mission of Australia to the United Nations. Thank you very much.

My name is Alistair McEachran. I'm representing Ambassador Larsen. Thank you, Excellencies. Critical technologies are reshaping the globe and transforming how our societies function in ways that are difficult to predict. While technology and AI offer transformative benefits, they also introduce parallel risks, expanding the threat landscape at a pace that challenges our traditional responses to terrorism. We must keep pace while building resilience against the exploitation of technologies by those who seek to do harm. I will highlight 3 priority areas for our collective response, first we must understand how emerging technologies are being misused. Generative AI is enabling the rapid production of extremist propaganda in multiple languages. Social media is amplifying grievance narratives, eroding trust in institutions, spreading hate, and creating a permissive environment for violence. Encrypted applications, gaming platforms, and AI-assisted tools are enabling more targeted recruitment and radicalization. Particularly of young people. As co-chair of the Global Counterterrorism Forum's Countering Violent Extremism Working Group with Indonesia, Australia is prioritizing efforts to counter youth radicalization on new platforms. Second, we must strengthen prevention. With the UN Office of Counterterrorism, Australia is supporting the Building Safer Online Gaming Communities initiative. This program equips young gamers and moderators in Southeast Asia with tools to prevent exploitation of gaming platforms and promote safer online environments. Third, we must continue to promote strong and effective national policy responses. This includes Australia's world-leading Under-16 Social Media Laws, placing responsibility on platforms to protect users at a critical stage of their development. These are supported by our strong legislative and regulatory framework. The Online Safety Act 2021 empowers the eSafety Commissioner to address and remove harmful content, including terrorism-related material. Regulation alone is not enough. Australia also promotes safety by design, encouraging technology companies and developers to embed safeguards against misuse from the earliest stages of AI development. Across all efforts, we remain committed to upholding international law, including human rights. Effective counter-terrorism responses must not only protect our security,. They must also safeguard the values that underpin it. Excellencies, the misuse of AI and emerging technologies is present and an accelerating threat. We must act collectively to share expertise and build capacity to ensure these technologies are used for good, not harm. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Australia, and I now give the floor the floor to Her Excellency Ambassador Laura Dubiti-Esser, Permanent Representative of Uruguay to the United Nations.

Buenas tardes. Good afternoon, Excellencies and delegates. I'm going to speak on behalf of the Ambassador and Permanent Representative of Uruguay. Uruguay would like to begin by thanking you for organizing this 4th High-Level Conference, and we value in particular the ability to have an exchange during Session 4. Tackling the improper use of artificial intelligence and emerging technologies in the fight against terrorism is undoubtedly one of the most complex challenges that we are facing today. From our point of view, we observe the need to balance the imperative of security with the full respect for international law. And in particular human rights. Uruguay, a country which has built its diplomatic tradition on the basis of dialogue, multilateralism, and strong institutions, maintains that technological innovation and the rule of law are not only compatible, but they should move forward harmoniously. Along these lines, the review of the Global Counterterrorist Strategy represents a key opportunity to consolidate a framework which incorporates accountability, transparency, and the observance of human rights as cross-cutting aspects in which would cut through technology and security. Furthermore, Uruguay promotes a collaborative approach which recognizes the different realities of every region. For us, it's a matter of priority to promote studies which should make it possible to understand the real capabilities of the different territories, as well as to promote the development of regional databases within existing legal frameworks. We also value the establishment of regional fora for the exchange of experiences and challenges, which would acknowledge the cultural and linguistic diversity. And we promote a constructive dialogue with the private sector and digital platforms as strategic allies. With respect to the protection of human rights, we feel it's crucial to carry out impact assessments on human rights. Prior to the implementation of any technological tool. And these assessments should be maintained throughout the lifecycle of that tool. Allow me to stress a fundamental aspect. Technology must be seen as a complement to human judgment and not as a replacement for it. AI results must be subject to properly trained human scrutiny. And for that, it's important to invest in the technical and legal training of teams, as well as robust oversight mechanisms. To conclude, Uruguay maintains that strategic capacity building should not be limited to the acquisition of advanced technology. It also involves a comprehensive commitment to the building of solid institutions, as well as transparent institutions which are respectful of human rights. We opt for an approach which combines the development of knowledge, cooperation with academia and industry, as well as the exchange of experiences between states. Chairman, the challenges that we have ahead of us are significant, but we trust that multilateral dialogue and international cooperation will allow us to chart a path which is balanced and sustainable. Thank you very much.
Thank you very much. Now I would like to invite His Excellency Mr. Ahmed Al Qazimi, Executive Director of HEDAYA.

Chair, shukran sayyid al-Rais. Thank you.
