Hidayah remains committed to supporting international efforts to address the risks and opportunities associated with emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence. Extremism, prior to becoming an act of violence, starts with ideology and communication. Terrorist groups integrate new technologies in their incitement, recruitment, indoctrination, and mobilization efforts. Hidayah's AI research showed that AI amplifies existing challenges by increasing its scale, speed, and reach. Radical and extremist content is adapted to become more mainstream and locally contextualized, making it harder to detect. One of the challenges we faced is the speed of these emerging technologies. By the time we understand one aspect of this technology, the threat has already evolved to something more complex. This year, Hedayat brought together governments, researchers, civil society organizations, and tech companies to bridge knowledge gaps and to provide evidence-based solutions. This resulted in identified positive opportunities to leverage AI for good, in our prevention efforts, such as assisting with content moderation, identifying trends and vulnerable vulnerabilities, help practitioners conduct large-scale analysis, build online resilience and counter narratives, and ensure stakeholders don't work in silos. While AI and gaming platforms bring new risks and amplify existing threats, many of the root causes of radicalization actually remain the same. Through our programs such as Tech to Protect and Skills for Resilience, Hedayat has worked with computer science students in Tunisia to translate our knowledge into practice, empower youth, and strengthen online resilience for them to develop their own creative solutions to counter radicalization within their local context. This also reminds us of the important nexus between the online and offline space. As threats are not solely defined within the digital space. Every act of radicalization online will have an offline consequence eventually, and vice versa. Grievances and vulnerabilities do tend to influence how receptive individuals are when engaging with extremist content online. In conclusion, I would like to share a concerning finding. We are witnessing that radical groups Terrorists are exploiting blind spots in online platforms whereby part of the radicalization process is done in one platform. The same individual is then lured to another platform where incitement to commit violence begins. A recent terrorist attack in Southeast Asia was carried out using exactly this method. Therefore, it is crucial for us to adapt, multilaterally align, enhance resilience, build digital literacy and youth community-led programs as we counter terrorism together. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. Al Qasimi. And now I give the floor to the final speaker in our list. And those who are unable to deliver their statement, we kindly ask them to email them to the Secretariat for publication. I now give the floor to Mr. Emmanuel Laprofido, Vice Chair of OSCE CCEPA CCT.

Thank you, dear Chair. I speak as Vice Chair of the Ad Hoc Committee on Countering Terrorism of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly. When we discuss artificial intelligence, we often begin with regulation. Regulation is necessary, but regulation alone is not enough. The real challenge is capacity. Terrorists and violent extremist actors are adapting quickly. They can use artificial intelligence to produce propaganda, create synthetic content, translate extremist messages, target vulnerable individuals, and exploit digital environments such as social media, gaming platforms, and encrypted messaging. Artificial intelligence does not create terrorist intent, but it can multiply terrorist capability. This is not about blaming institutions. It is a call for urgency and cooperation. Parliaments, governments, and public administrations must work together rapidly to build the awareness, legal tools, and operational capacity needed to respond effectively. For this reason, capacity building must develop in 5 directions. First, parliamentary capacity. Parliaments must be able to understand these technologies, assess their risk, update legal frameworks, and exercise democratic oversight. Second, law enforcement and judicial capacity. Police authorities, prosecutors, and judges need clear legal instruments, technical expertise, and stronger international cooperation to detect, investigate, and prosecute the malicious use of AI and emerging technologies for terrorist purposes. Third, technological and institutional capacity. Technological sovereignty means democratic capacity, the ability to understand, audit, and govern technologies that affect security, fundamental rights, and public debate. Fourth, prevention capacity. In the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly, our committee has focused on youth radicalization, artificial intelligence, media and information literacy, and online safety. Through the School Dialogue Initiative developed with the Next Wave Center, we engage directly with the student, teacher, local, local experts, and civil society. Two dialogues have already taken place, one in Pordenone, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Italy, and one in Cetinje, Montenegro, involving around 200 students aged 13 to 18. Their message was clear: young people are asking for more support, more protection, and more institutional responsibility. They are also asking us to make digital literacy a permanent, permanent part of education, not a one-off project. Fifth, international capacity. No country can face the challenge— this challenge alone. Terrorist networks, digital platforms, online propaganda, and financial flows are transnational. Our response must be equally coordinated through the United Nations, regional organizations, and parliamentary assemblies. To conclude, dear Chair, countering the misuse of AI is not only a security issue. It is a test of democratic readiness. If terrorist actors adapt faster than our institutions, they will exploit our weaknesses. But if we strengthen parliaments, law enforcement, schools, communities, and international cooperation, we can ensure that artificial intelligence serves security, freedom, and human dignity. Thank you.
Thank you very much. I thank all those who have taken the floor. The list of speakers is now exhausted, and then those who still have statements to give, please do so.

So now, Yes, let me just— I would like to thank all participants, special guests, and delegation for their insightful contribution and active participation. This session has highlighted both opportunities and challenges associated with the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies in the counterterrorism context. The discussion has underscored the importance of investing in the capacity building, strengthening international cooperation, and ensuring that innovation is accompanied by appropriate safeguards, accountability, and respect for international law and human rights. As technological change continues to accelerate, sustained dialogue and practical cooperation among member states, the United Nations system, academia, and other stakeholders will remain essential to preventing the misuse of emerging technologies for terrorist purposes. Closing is here. I will give the floor to my co-chair to close the session.

So once again, we'd like to thank all the participants for your presence and engagement. And please now stay, right? Or move to— Stay here for the closing session. So with this, session 4 of the high-level conference Dear participants, please take your seats.

We should start our closing session with which I assure you will be very important but very short. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues, I call to order the closing session of the 4th High-Level Conference of Heads of Counterterrorism Agencies of Member States. It is my honor to give the floor to the Chef de Cabinet, Mr. Courtney Rattray, who will be delivering remarks on behalf of the Deputy Secretary-General. Dear Chef de Cabinet, the floor is yours.

Excellencies, Under-Secretary-General Zouev, ladies and gentlemen, it's a pleasure for me to deliver these remarks on behalf of the Deputy Secretary-General. Let me begin by thanking the UN Office for Counter-Terrorism for convening this important conference and for its continued support to Member States in strengthening the international cooperation against terrorism. I also want to recognize the people in this room. You lead the agencies that disrupt terrorist activities, follow the financing, secure borders, and bring perpetrators to justice. Your work is carried out, as you know, under intense pressure, often with incomplete information and against networks moving faster than the law, always with the knowledge that lives are at stake. When your agencies succeed, much of that success is invisible. When something fails, The consequences are public and they are devastating. Therefore, my first message is one of recognition. Thank you for your service. Thank you for your commitment. Over these two days, you have examined a threat that evolves across conflict zones, criminal networks, and digital platforms, exploiting vulnerabilities Grievances, technology, and fear. As we approach the 9th review of the UN Global Counterterrorism Strategy and mark 20 years— 20 years since its adoption, we have a chance to strengthen its impact. The strategy recognized a fundamental truth that your experience confirms each and every day: lasting security cannot be achieved through enforcement measures alone. The balance that we strive to uphold is clear: protecting people from immediate threat, while reducing the conditions that allow terrorist groups to recruit, finance, move and hide. This Conference has shown how demanding that balance is. As you know firsthand, a cell can be dismantled, and another forms. A group can be weakened in one place and resurface in another. Where the underlying conditions persist, the threat simply regenerates. That is why prevention is not an alternative to your work; it is what makes its gains hold. Prevention deserves the same seriousness, investment, and attention as response. Building inclusive, resilient and sustainable societies is therefore central to lasting security. The 2030 Agenda provides the roadmap to invest in people, strengthen institutions, reduce inequalities, expand opportunity and leave no one behind. This requires partnership among Member States, the UN, regional organizations and civil society— partnership anchored in national ownership, local engagement, and a commitment to reach those most at risk. Ladies and gentlemen, this week also brought important voices into the room. Victims and survivors remind us of what is at stake. They carry the consequences of terrorism long after the headlines move on. Their rights— dignity and participation must remain central to policies and assistance. Women's organizations and women leaders are often among the first to recognize shifts within their communities, where trust is fraying, young people are being targeted and support is needed. Their participation makes counter-terrorism more grounded and credible. Young people and civil society are also an essential part of the work. A whole-of-society approach means including these actors in policy design and implementation, drawing on the knowledge needed to be as effective as possible. Friends, 20 years since the adoption of the Strategy, we have gained significant insight. We know that counter-terrorism is most effective when it is anchored in the rule of law, human rights, and in the trust of communities. We know that prevention works best when it is early, sustained, and is rooted in local realities. And we know that no one can address this threat alone. That means supporting the agencies protecting people every day, while ensuring that our collective response remains grounded in dignity, opportunity, and trust. The DSG remains firmly committed to this effort, alongside the Secretary-General, So rest assured that the UN Office of Counter-Terrorism and the wider United Nations system will continue to support Member States in carrying it forward. I thank you.

I would like to thank very much the Chef de Cabinet for delivering the remarks on behalf of the Deputy Secretary-General, and I thank the Deputy Secretary-General for her unwavering commitment to our collective efforts in preventing and countering terrorism. The Deputy Secretary-General had been instrumental in bringing into sharper focus the need to support especially the efforts of member states in Africa, where, as we just discussed, terrorism has been taking a growing and devastating toll. We are especially grateful for her leadership in advocating for a comprehensive approach that recognizes how sustainable development, human rights, peace and security are synergetically interlinked. I will now deliver a brief summary to conclude this high-level conference. It will be— first of all, you should be happy, it will be really short, first of all, and secondly, unlike the opening session when I used my four official UN languages, our interpreters won't be tortured, I will speak only English this time. So, of course, first of all, I would like to express my sincere gratitude to all co-chairs, special guests, panelists, and participants who contributed to the richness of our discussions over these two days. Obviously, I would like to thank all the United Nations colleagues from different UN agencies which participate in the Secretary-General's Global Counterterrorism Compact, which we were asked to coordinate from UNOCT, but every agency made a very valuable contribution, and obviously, on my right I have Assistant Secretary General from GCAM. We have to thank this department for all their support and they were very instrumental. As you know, probably, we had altogether during these 4 days, we had more than 45 events in different conference rooms, not only the plenary which is here and— well, I cannot resist to tell that You know, initially we announced that the closing will be in the General Assembly Hall, but the Fifth Committee is a very powerful committee which approves— I mean, of the General Assembly, which approves our budget and staff tables, I mean, all this. And in addition, unlike UNCT, they are General Assembly main committee. I mean, you know, so they are very kindly and softly but evicted us. From this wonderful hall, but at least I am happy that you've heard the Secretary-General, Antonio Guterres, to address you in this beautiful environment of this historic, I would say, conference room of the General Assembly. Well, since I mentioned this, of course, even in absentia, but I hope the Chef de Cabinet will convey this message from all of us, I would like to thank Mr. Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations, not only for addressing, but as you remember, he stayed, he stayed very long, I mean, you know, and listening to the whole opening session, and I hope it was very important for all of us, not only keynote address, but his steadfast leadership and support for the counterterrorism work of for the United Nations system, which myself personally, but my office feels every day, and obviously it comes from his executive office, from the chef de cabinet, and from DSG, as I said. I mean, you know, the perspective and insight shared throughout these two days must not remain within these walls. We stand ready to support member states and all our partners in taking forward the ideas, recommendations, and commitments raised during this— your deliberation and our discussions. Let this conference stand as a renewed call to action and a demonstration of the enduring importance of multilateral cooperation in the face of the evolving terrorist threats. Last but not least, I would like to remind you that, as you probably remember, tomorrow General Assembly will not only review but hopefully approve the 9th edition of the Global Counterterrorism Strategy, which is a guiding policy document for all Global Compact entities, including obviously UNOCT. With this, the 4th High-Level Conference of Heads of Counterterrorism Agencies of Member States is hereby officially closed.
